 7-Eleven makes its Korean menu a 7-episode Instagram K-drama
 Seven 60-second episodes weave convenience-store romance into a food campaign, with item-specific deals running alongside the story.
 Zoe Park 
 30 Oct 2026 
 • 5 min read 
 ✦

 ↓ 
 A late-night stop at 7-Eleven sounds like a small errand, but in a K-drama it can become the scene where romance gets complicated. A quick meal, an awkward encounter and a reason to come back can provide enough material for the next episode. That is the familiar storytelling language behind the retailer's new Flavors of Korea promotion. In its October 28 announcement , 7-Eleven outlined a seven-episode short drama that will appear on Instagram and TikTok alongside a temporary Korean-inspired food menu. The series is called A Convenient Love , as confirmed by a teaser shared through the brand's official Instagram account. Rather than bring an existing TV property into stores, 7-Eleven is making its own fictional romance. The story follows two classmates whose lives keep intersecting during late-night snack runs. Their relationship gives viewers something to follow between menu promotions, without requiring a full-length television episode.

 How A Convenient Love turns a snack run into a series 
 A Convenient Love is designed as a sequence, not a single food commercial. Its seven vertical episodes run about 60 seconds each, with new installments planned for Mondays and Thursdays between November 2 and November 23. The videos will appear on the 7-Eleven and Speedway Instagram and TikTok accounts. The Instagram teaser introduces the premise through rivals, romance and late-night visits. That combination suits the compact drama format: the story does not need a complicated setting when the same convenience store can host each encounter. Repeated visits are both a plausible romantic device and a recognizable part of the retail experience. Director Danny Lee described how closely the story and setting were built together. "We built 7 vertical episodes around it and shot all of them in a real 7-Eleven," he said in the retailer's announcement. It is a deliberate choice to keep the fictional world inside the store. Instead of interrupting the story for a product shot, 7-Eleven can make a snack part of why the characters meet. Whether audiences actually follow the entire series remains to be seen; the campaign is only at its teaser stage.

 Each episode will focus on a menu item and carry a limited-time offer for that food. The structure gives viewers two possible reasons to return: to see what happens to the classmates and to discover the next featured snack. The Korean-inspired lineup includes bibigo Spicy Chicken Dumplings, bibigo Korean BBQ-Style Pizza, Gochujang Boneless Wings, K Town Chicken Salad Sando, Korean-Style BBQ Sauced Taquito, K Noodle Salad and a Korean-style BBQ sausage. A Seoul Style Sweet Heat Chicken Sandwich is also available at participating Raise the Roost locations.
 7-Eleven says a ten-piece serving of the bibigo Spicy Chicken Dumplings is US$5, while eight Gochujang Boneless Wings are also US$5 at participating locations. Separately, qualifying 7Rewards and Speedy Rewards members can add a 20-ounce Coke or Pepsi for US$1 with certain food purchases during the promotional period.
 These offers make the fictional series more than an awareness play. A viewer can see a product during a dramatic moment, then encounter a related offer in a real store. The brand has not disclosed whether that combination improves visits or sales, so it is better understood as the design of the campaign, not a proven result.
 Why K-drama storytelling is becoming a brand format 
 The Korean drama reference here is about the storytelling form, not the use of a licensed show or celebrity. A familiar genre supplies tension, repeated encounters and characters to follow. The product becomes part of that world without needing to carry every moment of the plot. 7-Eleven is not alone in trying the format. Colgate Optic White Purple used a six-part TikTok K-drama called The Purple café across Asia Pacific, placing toothpaste inside scenes about social awkwardness and confidence. Mastercard also used a three-part romantic microdrama to make payment safety an entertainment storyline in Southeast Asia. The difference for 7-Eleven is the retail connection built into its release schedule. Colgate used a beauty product as a character-level plot device; 7-Eleven links each new chapter to a menu item and a timely food offer. The comparison is about creative mechanics, not campaign performance, for which comparable results have not been published. There is another useful distinction. A K-drama-inspired miniseries is not automatically a fan community. The retailer is borrowing storytelling conventions that some viewers already recognize, but the teaser's existence does not establish popularity, repeat viewing or audience response. Those are outcomes to evaluate after the episodes appear.
 What this means for marketers 
 The campaign illustrates a way to make a limited-time product range feel like an ongoing story. Its effectiveness will depend on what happens between episodes and whether food offers turn that attention into store visits.
 1. Give people a reason to return. A sequence of connected episodes offers a stronger follow-up than a single product reveal. The promise of another chapter is part of the creative idea.
 2. Make products useful to the plot. A convenience-store snack is believable in the characters' world. The food does not have to be a separate advertisement if it contributes to the scene.
 3. Connect entertainment with an action. A menu-specific discount makes the next episode relevant beyond viewing alone. The conversion path is clear, although its results have not been disclosed.
 4. Avoid mistaking genre recognition for proven fandom. Familiar K-drama conventions may help the content feel understandable, but measured audience behavior is needed before calling the approach successful.
 One of the more interesting aspects is that the store itself is both the set and the destination. The fictional late-night snack run mirrors the practical visit the brand hopes to encourage. For marketers, the larger question is whether episodic storytelling can give everyday products enough narrative weight that people choose to follow them. 7-Eleven has established the premise and release calendar. The real test starts when viewers can watch the first episode on November 2.
